land.text: the Pyu land still outside Pagan in 1044 as Cliopatria draws it: Sri Ksetra near Pyay and the southern dry zone, and the Mu valley around Halin; the Pagan page's 1044 districts (Mandalay, Meiktila, Myingyan, Kyaukse, Yamethin, Magwe, Sagaing and the riverine parts of Minbu and Pakkoku) do not include them, and it puts Pyus 'to the south and the west'

successors.note: 'By Anawrahta's accession in 1044, Pagan had grown into a small principality'; the empire followed 'in the 1050s and 1060s'. The Pyu 'by the early 13th century, had largely assumed the Burman ethnicity'.

capitals.name: Beikthano
capitals.note: 'Coordinates: 20°0′14″N 95°22′46″E', 'near present-day Taungdwingyi'; 'the city may be the first capital of a culturally and perhaps even politically uniform state in the history of Burma'. A network of city-states had no single capital; the premier city is given.

capitals.name: Halin (Halingyi)
capitals.note: 'founded in the 1st century AD', earliest gate artefacts 'radiocarbon dated to 70 CE'; 'Halin was superseded by Sri Ksetra circa 7th century' (Pyu page). Coordinates from the Hanlin, Burma page: '22°28′54″N 95°48′00″E' (near Shwebo, Sagaing Region); the page also says Hanlin 'was established by the Pyu people only during the 1st or 2nd century BC' and 'was the largest Pyu city until the 9th century AD', which disagrees with the Pyu page's dates.

capitals.name: Sri Ksetra (Hmawza, near Pyay)
capitals.note: Infobox capitals: Sri Ksetra, Halin, Beikthano, Pinle, Binnaka. Sri Ksetra 'retained that status until the Mranma arrived in the 9th century' and 'declined in prominence around the ninth century AD' (Sri Ksetra page); the same page also says 'With the fall of Sri Ksetra in the mid-ninth century, king Anawrahta opened the stūpa and removed the relic' (a tradition about the relic, no cause given); kept to 1044 for want of a later premier city. Coordinates are the researcher's (Hmawza).

correction.text: the earliest Pyu cities: Beikthano ('Beikthano founded: c. 180 BCE'; remains 'from 200 BCE to 100 CE') in the Minbu–Magway plain, and Maingmaw and Binnaka in the Kyaukse plains ('tentatively dated to the first millennium BCE')

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria begins the Pyu in 84 CE but the infobox gives 'Earliest Pyu presence in Upper Myanmar (Burma): c. 2nd century BCE' and 'Beikthano founded: c. 180 BCE'; Halin follows in the 1st century AD. Beikthano is not in the gazetteer (20.00 N 95.38 E, Magway Region).

Cliopatria's 84 shape, 116,187 km2 in shapes.csv (about 103,700 km2 in the gazetteer's cells), kept for 84–849 as Cliopatria dates it. 'longer than wide, stretching from Sri Ksetra in the south to Halin in the north', with the Mu valley, the Kyaukse plains and the Minbu region; Tang records '18 Pyu states, nine of which were walled cities, covering 298 districts'. No infobox area to compare (the infobox 'Area' reads 'Sites of Pyu city-states in the Irrawaddy valley'). Halin and the Mu valley stay inside it: the 832 Nanzhao attack is a contested zone (ledger), not a loss. The 763 conquest of the upper Irrawaddy lies north of the shape (Kachin, 0 cells of overlap with the gazetteer).

111,322 km2; the 5,000 km2 removed is Cliopatria's first Pagan shape, 'Founding of kingdom: 23 December 849' (infobox), 'Pyinbya fortified the city in 849 AD'. Halin and the Mu valley stay in the shape (no loss in 832: the attack is a raid, see the ledger); 70 cells, about 17,700 km2, of an 80 km circle around Halin lie inside it.

95,230 km2; Cliopatria's Pagan grows to 26,800 km2 in 860. No page dates this step ('Radiocarbon dating of Pagan's walls points to c. 980 at the earliest'); kept as Cliopatria's staging of the Burman settlement 'in the 830s and 840s', unverified. Early Pagan Kingdom page: Pyinbya 'r. 846–886'; 'The region of Pagan received waves of Burman settlements in the mid-to-late 9th century'; it dates no step in 860.

77,433 km2; Pagan at 44,600 km2 from 960. 'Burmans took leadership by the late 10th century'; the shape stands. Early Pagan Kingdom page: the principality was 'one of many competing city-states in the Pyu realm until the late 10th century' 'when the principality began absorbing its surrounding states'; Nyaung-u Sawrahan 'r. 956–1001'.

Years only: to December 1044, when 'a Pagan prince named Anawrahta came to power'; Cliopatria ends the Pyu in 1045 and the Pyu infobox says 'Rise of the Pagan Kingdom: c. 1050 CE'. The remaining Pyu land goes to Pagan (identity.successors): Cliopatria's Pagan shape of 1046 (122,646 km2) is about Pagan's 960 shape (44,586 km2) plus this remainder (77,433 km2), so Halin and the Mu valley pass to Pagan with it. Against the Pagan page's 1044 districts: Beikthano and the Minbu plain lie in Pagan's 960 shape, not in this remainder; Mandalay and Yamethin have their centres inside the remainder, an edge difference within the precision of the shape.

region.text: the earliest Pyu cities: Beikthano ('Beikthano founded: c. 180 BCE'; remains 'from 200 BCE to 100 CE') in the Minbu–Magway plain, and Maingmaw and Binnaka in the Kyaukse plains ('tentatively dated to the first millennium BCE')

ledger.note: c. 180 BCE: the Pyu build Beikthano, the first walled city of the Irrawaddy dry zone. Infobox 'Beikthano founded: c. 180 BCE'; 'In about the 2nd century BCE' the Pyu entered the Irrawaddy valley; Beikthano's remains 'date from 200 BCE to 100 CE' and its walls are 'radiocarbon dated to a period between 180 BCE and 610 CE' (Beikthano page). A network of city-states drawn as one polity; stateless land before (rule 8).

70: Halin founded in the Mu valley and becomes the premier Pyu city. Halin was 'founded in the 1st century AD', its earliest gate artefacts 'radiocarbon dated to 70 CE'; Beikthano suffered 'an earthquake ... around the 2nd century AD and a war around the 3rd and 4th century AD' (Beikthano page). The order of precedence between the cities is the researcher's reading. The Hanlin, Burma page differs: Hanlin 'was established by the Pyu people only during the 1st or 2nd century BC' and 'was the largest Pyu city until the 9th century AD'; 70 stays as the date of the earliest radiocarbon-dated gate artefacts (Pyu page).

7th century: Sri Ksetra supersedes Halin. 'Halin was superseded by Sri Ksetra circa 7th century'; placed at the Vikrama epoch of 638 for want of a dated year. Xuanzang (648) and Yijing (675) name Sri Ksetra; its material is 'dated between the seventh and ninth centuries AD' (Sri Ksetra page). Hanlin, Burma page: 'Subsequently, Sri Ksetra near Pyay became a more prominent city'; Pyu page: 'Sri Ksetra likely overtook Halin as the premier Pyu city by the 7th or 8th century'. No page gives a year.

638: the Vikrama dynasty of Sri Ksetra launches the Burmese calendar. 'Vikrama Dynasty launched the calendar on 22 March 638'; infobox 'Burmese calendar begins: 22 March 638'. Same polity, same colour (rule 2).
739: Duttabaung founds the second Sri Ksetra dynasty. Infobox '2nd Sri Ksetra Dynasty founded: 25 March 739'.

region.text: 'the upper Irrawaddy Valley', read as the Irrawaddy's upper basin in Kachin State

ledger.note: 763: Nanzhao takes the upper Irrawaddy valley. 'By 763, the Nanzhao king Ko-lo-feng had conquered the upper Irrawaddy Valley'; Nanzhao raids began 'as early as 754 or 760'. The valley is read as Kachin State, which lies north of Cliopatria's Pyu shape (gazetteer check: 0 cells of overlap; the shape ends at 23.96 N), so the loss lies outside the drawn realm and changes nothing in it; the earlier circle at 96.2 E 24.6 N (150 km) overlapped about 8,000 km2 of the shape's north and was replaced. The Nanzhao page does not credit Geluofeng with this conquest; it gives his walled city in Dadan (Hkamti Long) without a date.

region.text: Halin (Halingyi) and the Mu valley, 'destroying the city of Halin in 832'

ledger.note: 832: Nanzhao attacks and sacks Halin. Nanzhao is credited with 'conquering the Pyu city-states in the 820s and destroying the city of Halin in 832' and brought back 'three thousand prisoners of war'; by 808 its king took 'the title of Piaoxin (驃信), meaning Ruler of the Pyu'. The Pyu page calls the attacks raids that 'significantly weakened the Pyu states', says 'no firm indications at Sri Ksetra or at any other Pyu site exist to suggest a violent overthrow', and dates human activity at Halin to c. 870; no page opened names a Nanzhao garrison, governor or tribute, so the Mu valley is drawn as contested, not lost. Halin is not in the gazetteer (22.48 N 95.80 E).

835: the last recorded Nanzhao attack at Halin. 'They returned to Halin in 835 and carried off many prisoners', and 'in 835, they subdued Michen' in lower Burma; none of the pages opened records Nanzhao troops or officials in the dry zone afterwards (the 849 settlement on the Irrawaddy was 'possibly to help Nanzhao pacify the area'), so Halin is drawn Pyu again. A de facto end of the fighting, no treaty.

region.text: Pagan (Bagan) and its surroundings on the Irrawaddy

ledger.note: 849: Pagan founded on the Irrawaddy. 'Founding of kingdom: 23 December 849' (infobox); 'Pyinbya fortified the city in 849 AD' (the text adjusts the chronicle date to 876); 'large numbers of Burman warriors and their families first entered the Pyu realm in the 830s and 840s'. The Nanzhao page: 'In 849, a fortified settlement was established along the Irrawaddy River, possibly to help Nanzhao pacify the area.' Cliopatria's Pagan row begins 850 with 5,368 km2.

region.text: the land Cliopatria moves from the Pyu to Pagan in 860

ledger.note: 860: Pagan's principality grows. Cliopatria's Pagan shape rises to 26,800 km2 in 860; no page dates this step ('Radiocarbon dating of Pagan's walls points to c. 980 at the earliest'; 'the Kyaukse agricultural basin's development in the 10th and 11th centuries'). A bridging event at Cliopatria's year. Early Pagan Kingdom page: Pyinbya 'r. 846–886'; 'The region of Pagan received waves of Burman settlements in the mid-to-late 9th century'; it dates no step in 860.

region.text: the land Cliopatria moves from the Pyu to Pagan in 960

ledger.note: 960: the Burmans lead the dry zone. Early Pagan Kingdom page: Pagan 'was one of many competing city-states in the Pyu realm until the late 10th century' 'when the principality began absorbing its surrounding states'; Pyu page: 'Burmans took leadership by the late 10th century'. Cliopatria's Pagan grows to 44,600 km2 in 960, a size close to the Early Pagan page's 1044 principality (about 320 km north to south by 130 km east to west). No page gives the year 960: a bridging event at Cliopatria's year.

region.text: the Pyu land still outside Pagan in 1044 as Cliopatria draws it: Sri Ksetra near Pyay and the southern dry zone, and the Mu valley around Halin; the Pagan page's 1044 districts (Mandalay, Meiktila, Myingyan, Kyaukse, Yamethin, Magwe, Sagaing and the riverine parts of Minbu and Pakkoku) do not include them, and it puts Pyus 'to the south and the west'

ledger.note: 1044: Anawrahta comes to power at Pagan; the Pyu cities pass under Pagan. 'In December 1044, a Pagan prince named Anawrahta came to power'; 'By Anawrahta's accession in 1044, Pagan had grown into a small principality' around Kyaukse and Minbu; 'By the mid-1050s, Anawrahta's reforms had turned Pagan into a regional power'; 'until the 1050s and 1060s when King Anawrahta founded the Pagan Empire'. The Pyu infobox gives 'Rise of the Pagan Kingdom: c. 1050 CE'; Cliopatria ends the Pyu in 1045. The Pagan page puts 'the riverine portions of Minbu and Pakkoku' in Pagan by 1044, so the region text no longer lists the Minbu plain (or Beikthano, which lies in Pagan's 960 shape); Halin and the Mu valley pass to Pagan in this event, as Cliopatria's Pagan shape of 1046 has them.

wars.name: Nanzhao invasions of the Pyu (832–835)

zones.text: Halin and the Mu valley, 'destroying the city of Halin in 832'

wars.outcome: Halin destroyed and 3,000 prisoners taken in 832; 'in 835, they subdued Michen (near the mouth of the Ayeyarwady River in lower Burma)' and 'returned to Halin in 835 and carried off many prisoners'. Drawn as a contested zone 832–835 (ledger), not as a loss of land. The Pyu realm never recovered: 'repeated attacks by the Nanzhao kingdom of Yunnan between the 750s and 830s AD' (Pagan page).
wars.note: Michen was a lower-Burma (Mon) polity, not a Pyu city; not drawn here. Whether Nanzhao ruled the Pyu after 832 is not settled by the pages (Nanzhao page: 'conquering the Pyu city-states in the 820s'; Pyu page: raids, 'no firm indications ... of a violent overthrow').

certainty.note: A network of walled cities with no recorded frontier; the outer limit is the Irrawaddy dry zone from Halin to Sri Ksetra. The Pagan boundary 849–1044 follows Cliopatria's staging and is the softest of all.

sources.title: Pyu city-states
sources.note: Identity, infobox dates (c. 180 BCE Beikthano, 22 March 638, 25 March 739, c. 1050), the cities, the extent, the Nanzhao raids ('By 763 ... conquered the upper Irrawaddy Valley'; 'in 832, the Nanzhao warriors overran the Pyu country'; raids that 'significantly weakened the Pyu states'; 'no firm indications ... of a violent overthrow'), Halin's activity to c. 870, the Burman arrival. No infobox area (the 'Area' line reads 'Sites of Pyu city-states in the Irrawaddy valley').

sources.title: Pagan Kingdom
sources.note: Pagan's founding 23 December 849, the Burman arrival in the 830s–840s, Anawrahta's accession in December 1044 and the empire of the 1050s–1060s, Halin's activity to c. 870.

sources.title: Sri Ksetra Kingdom
sources.note: Sri Ksetra's dating (7th–9th centuries), the 638 epoch, Xuanzang 648 and Yijing 675, decline in the 9th century; the page's chronicle dates (444 BC, 94 AD, 107 AD) are legend. Reopened in the repair pass: silent on Nanzhao and on a 739 dynasty.

sources.title: Nanzhao
sources.note: The 832 destruction of Halin, 835 Michen, the title Piaoxin (808), the 849 fortified settlement; silent on Geluofeng's upper-Irrawaddy conquest and on a Pyu vassalage.

sources.title: Beikthano
sources.note: Coordinates 20°0′14″N 95°22′46″E near Taungdwingyi, dating 200 BCE–100 CE and walls 180 BCE–610 CE, 300 ha, earthquake and war, sacked by Sri Ksetra.

sources.title: Early Pagan Kingdom
sources.note: Repair pass. The 849 founding, Pyinbya r. 846–886, Nyaung-u Sawrahan r. 956–1001, 'competing city-states ... until the late 10th century', the 1044 principality (districts; about 320 km by 130 km). Dates no step at 860 or 960.

sources.title: Hanlin, Burma
sources.note: Repair pass. Coordinates 22°28′54″N 95°48′00″E, 541.4 ha, founded 1st or 2nd century BC, largest Pyu city until the 9th century AD, Sri Ksetra 'subsequently' more prominent; silent on 832 and c. 870. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halin is only a disambiguation page.)

notes:
Cliopatria row 'Pyu City-States' 84–1045 (5 shapes) kept as one dossier: the brief flagged 961 years as 'probably successive states', but the pages describe one network of city-states (Beikthano, Halin, Sri Ksetra, Maingmaw, Binnaka) with a shared culture, script and calendar, whose premier city moved from Beikthano to Halin to Sri Ksetra; the Vikrama (638) and second Sri Ksetra (739) dynasties are rename events, not new states. No split. Corrections: start c. 180 BCE (new keyframe, Beikthano) instead of 84 CE; end December 1044 (Anawrahta) instead of 1045.

Repair pass (review of 2026-10-18): the first version removed Halin's region from 832 (a loss to Nanzhao) but kept Cliopatria's 850, 860, 960 and 1040 shapes, which contain it, so the map gave Halin back with no gain. After reopening the Pyu, Nanzhao, Pagan, Early Pagan and Hanlin pages the 832 loss and its keyframe are dropped: the pages describe raids (Pyu page: 'a series of raids' that 'significantly weakened the Pyu states', 'no firm indications ... of a violent overthrow', human activity at Halin to c. 870), none names a garrison or tribute, and Cliopatria's Pagan shape of 1046 carries Halin and the Mu valley, so they stay Pyu to 1044. The 832–835 attack is a contest_start/contest_end pair with Nanzhao. The 763 loss now names Kachin State (0 cells of overlap with the 84 shape), which is outside the drawn realm.

Unsettled: the 84 CE start Cliopatria chose has no counterpart on the pages (the Sakra Era 'adopted in the Pyu realm in 80 CE' is the nearest date); the 860 and 960 shrinkages are Cliopatria's staging of Pagan's growth, which no page dates (the Early Pagan page says only 'until the late 10th century' and gives Pyinbya r. 846–886; confidence 1); whether Nanzhao ruled the Pyu: the Nanzhao page has 'conquering the Pyu city-states in the 820s' and the title 'Ruler of the Pyu' from 808, the Pyu and Sri Ksetra pages say raids or nothing, and no page gives a garrison, tribute or an end date, so no vassal tint is recorded here (the Nanzhao dossier may decide otherwise); when Halin was the premier city (the Hanlin, Burma page: founded 1st or 2nd century BC, largest until the 9th century AD; the Pyu page: radiocarbon 70 CE, superseded by Sri Ksetra by the 7th or 8th century; confidence 1); the fate of Beikthano and Sri Ksetra between 832 and 1044 (Sri Ksetra 'declined in prominence around the ninth century AD'); Michen (835) is a lower-Burma polity without a Cliopatria row (Mon city-states, 'c. 825–1057' in the Pagan navbox), a counterpart another dossier may need.

Gazetteer names used that it lacks: Beikthano (place, 20.00 N 95.38 E, Magway Region), Halin (place, 22.48 N 95.80 E per the Hanlin, Burma page; Sagaing Region, also Halingyi/Hanlin).

Pages: all opened loaded. The Seshat pages were not opened (no SeshatID on the row).
